Boycott of Christian businesses from May 1914; many emigrated. Russian occupation from 8 March 1916 to early 1918. In early 1918 returning Turkish bands destroyed Rize; inhabitants compelled to leave for Russia; churches, schools and houses demolished; only four Greeks remained (Patriarchate 1919: 113; all via Topalidis, 'A History of Rize').

Mines: the sancak had at one stage 37 argentiferous lead mines and 6 copper mines (pontosworld, after Malliaris); the mines declined after 1829 and were abandoned in the 1850s; the Greek mining masters (archimetallourgoi) were exempt from normal taxes for mining, smelting and charcoal work, and the Phytianos family supplied miners across Anatolia and the Caucasus (Topalidis, Crypto-Christians, after Bryer). Miners left for the new mines of Akdağ Madeni and Ergani (Argoni), and after the war of 1829 for South Russia, Nicomedia, Mesopotamia and other mines 'from Tiflis to Akdağ and the Taurus' (pontosworld, after Malliaris). notes: Group record, to be counted once with or instead of its villages (CAMS lists Kromni as a section, with 10 hamlets as entries, under the district of Trebizond; the hamlets are separate records). Andreadis 1995 (via Topalidis 2024) counts 15 Kromni settlements, several with sub-quarters. Kaza Torul: pontosworld says Kromni was under the kaimakam of Torul (Ardasa) and the mutasarrıf of Argyroupolis. Turkish forms: Kurum, Krom, Korom, Korum, Eskikiran (pontosworld). Crypto-Christians: the Kromlides; the first Kromniot to declare himself Orthodox, Petros Sideropoulos, did so at Trebizond on 14 May 1856, and declarations went on until c. 1910 (Topalidis, Crypto-Christians, after Bryer 2006). The 1857 'Kromni petition' covered a wider area: 55,755 people in 58 settlements, c. 31% (17,260) crypto-Christian (same source). Pontosworld says only 250 residents were left just before the 1923 exchange and that no Turks lived in Kromni until 1914 (unsourced). In 1929 Talbot Rice saw c. 400 ruined houses and about a dozen Turks (via Topalidis). Kromni is now the Krom quarter of Yağlıdere village (PTT) and largely abandoned (pontosworld: 'deserted'). Kromni Castle (Kurum Kale) stands above the ruins on the Kolat Dağları (Bryer & Winfield). Legend of settlers fleeing the coast after 1461 (pontosworld) not used as origin.

fate_1914_1923: Defended itself for several weeks, repelling bands more than once, and was saved (1918) (Patriarchate 1919, p. 114; printed 'Santa'). April 1915: 50 men taken into labour battalions, nearly all died; from 1916 an armed band under Euklidis Kourtidis (80-100 men) held the passes; 6-12 September 1921 Kemalist troops occupied Ishananton, Pinatanton and Terzanton and deported the villagers via Hunuz to Erzurum (and c. 200 on to Erzincan): 370 reached Hunuz and fewer than 200 returned by January 1923; the band and c. 300-400 women and children held out in the mountains until the exchange; survivors went to Greece (Nea Santa, Kilkis) and some to the USSR (Topalidis, 'Santa, Pontos After 1914', after Fotiadis 2019)

Other quarters named around Santa: Alainton, Ftelen, Garakotil, Haratsanton, Kopalanton (Goballı), Ypapanti (Topalidis). Mining until the mid-19th century. Santa ruins declared a protected site in 1999. Wikipedia (en) speaks of 13 quarters and over 5,000 people (no year).

Ottoman register no. 387 (1530) and the 1928 village list give the name Sevkar/Sevker (Nişanyan). An anonymous reader's note in Nişanyan's index says the village was wholly Christian in 1530, had 15 Muslim and 16 Christian households in 1642, and that its Orthodox spoke mostly Turkish until the early 19th century; it gives no source and is uncorroborated, so the language stays unknown. Bryer & Winfield's Karakaya may be another entry's village: Nişanyan's only Karakaya in Gümüşhane province (40.2921, 39.4639) lies 25 km east of Evren and 1.4 km from another entry's point. Possible duplicate with another entry; not merged. Two identifications disagree. Kiepert's map (1902–12) marks 'Mavrolíthi' at Evren (Şiran), and Nişanyan follows it. Bryer & Winfield (1985, p. 171) write that there are said to be no traces of the church at Mavrolithi '(now Karakaya)', east of the Cheriana valley, citing Kandilaptis (Χρονικά του Πόντου 3, 1946) and villagers' reports. The CAMS list has Μαυρολίθ' and Καράκαγια as two villages of Cheriana. The point stays at Evren; see another entry.

population: 17000 persons (1913) [pontosworld.com 'Kerasus - Giresun' (no source given; total c. 30,000: 17,000 Greeks, 3,000 Armenians, 7,000 Turks, 3,000 others)] | 14000 persons (1921) [Black Book 1922, narrative 'A few short notes...' (about 14,000 Greek inhabitants of Kerazond before the July 1921 deportation)] | 500 families (1870) [Ioannidis 1870, p. 217, Part Β′ «Στατιστικὴ τῆς χώρας» (chs. Η′–Ι′)]
churches: St Nicholas (with belltower); Transfiguration of the Saviour (Metamorphosis); others survive as buildings: the 'Gogora' church (now the archaeological museum) and the Kırkharman church (Wikipedia, 'Giresun'); a chapel of St Panteleimon and the 'hills of St Demetrius' appear in Ottoman-era captions
fate_1914_1923: Boycott, requisitions and arrests of merchants in 1916 (one died in custody); on 28 December 1916 three officers came to evacuate the town and 60, then 50 more, leading families were listed for expulsion from 1 January, but this was averted after the Metropolitan's appeal (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 102–108; printed 'Kerassounda'). 1916: Topal Osman blackmailed Orthodox Greeks and, for a fee, shipped some illegally to Russia; July 1916 he arrested men accused of trying to flee by sea and three wealthy merchants (Ioannis Deligiorgis died in custody); he was court-martialled (Sigalas 2026 (as cited on Wikipedia), 'Topal Osman'). 1919: Topal Osman, elected mayor, charged by the local Defence of Rights committee to act against Greek guerrillas (same). On the night of 13 August 1920 he imprisoned all the Christian men of Giresun; every evening five or six were taken out and shot until the community paid a ransom of 300,000 Turkish lira (Morris & Ze'evi 2019, p. 401). July 1921: the male population deported to Harput (Mamuret-ul-Aziz) and Elbistan; of about 14,000 Greeks of Kerazond only about 4,000 women and children remained (Black Book 1922, Greek advocacy). Morris & Ze'evi 2019, p. 413: in 1921 most Pontic Greeks of Giresun and Tirebolu were killed or deported. Survivors left in the exchange; refugees founded Nea Kerasounta (Preveza) among other villages.
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

location_source: GeoNames search, geonames.org: 'Keşap', Keşap, Giresun

fate_1914_1923: Named among the villages of the Kerasous region expelled by the end of 1916 (35,000 people with the Tripoli region), sent to Karahisar and dispersed; many died in six months of wandering (Patriarchate 1919, p. 107; printed 'Kassiopi'; probable identification: as in the Black Book; the record itself marks Kassiopi = Keşap as unconfirmed). Deported in winter 1916–17: 330 people listed for 'Kassiopi' (Kerasounda sub-district) in the Greek Legation's table of the Kerasous district, deportations to January 1917 (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 67; probable identification: as in the Black Book's 'Kassiopi', whose identity with Keşap is unconfirmed). Kerasous district, district-level account: after the Russian capture of Trebizond (1916) Turkish refugees brought cholera and typhus to the villages; on the governor's orders 38 villages (c. 23,000 people) were evacuated within 24 hours, without food, clothing or goods (report of Lavrentios, Metropolitan of Chaldia, 7 Feb 1917). A Greek report of 21 Apr 1917 says 88 Greek villages were evacuated and burned Dec 1916 - Feb 1917 and the people driven to the Ankara vilayet in winter, about a quarter dying on the way (it prints '300,000' deportees, impossible for this district). Both via the Encyclopedia of Pontic Hellenism vol. 2, as transcribed by imoph.org 2017 Part B. July 1921: men deported to Harput and Elbistan (Black Book 1922). No village-specific record found. The Tripoli deportees of 1916-17 were marched through Keşap (Sakkas, via imoph.org Part D).

fate_1914_1923: [Chaldie, pp. 106–107] Surrounded after Yol-Aghiz (late 1916) and evacuated 'by the same means'; the acting governor Nihad Bey withheld government bread from 2,000 Tripoli refugees camped by the Ak-sou river. fate_1914_1923: After the villages were emptied the townspeople bought time by hauling 200 tons of supplies a month to Mesudiye for the vali Cemal Azmi; the Russian fleet shelled the town on 19 August, and expulsion began in September 1917, the people scattered over the Sivas and Kastamonu vilayets except about 2,500 who went by sea to Trebizond and Russia (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 125–126; printed 'Ordou'). Greek notables deported Dec 1916 (VGM). Order of 20 Jul 1917 to remove men 16-50 by 25 Jul; c. 10,000 exiles gathered at Ordu, c. 2,000 taken off by a Russian warship in Aug 1917 (NYT 7 Apr 1918). After the Russian bombardment (Aug 1917) c. 2,500 left with the Russians for Trebizond and the Caucasus; the rest were expelled c. two months later to Sivas and Kastamonu (PW article). Second deportation from 1 Sep 1917; Saltsis gives the route Mesudiye - İsketir - Senne - Niksar - Erbaa, where c. 40% died (VGM). Men deported in waves 1921; bishop Polykarpos exiled to Ankara 1920/21; Circassians settled after evacuation; exit port 1922-23 (VGM).
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

Kaza invaded by Osman Ağa's bands, 'the same atrocities' as Tirebolu and Bulancak, c. 1921 (Black Book pp. 20-21, via greek-genocide.net). Halo (2000) describes a family deported south from Fatsa in spring 1920. About 300 people awaited passage in March 1923 (VGM Kaza Ordu). Exchanged 1923; many settled in Pieria (Trilofos).

language_basis: PW 'Unye (Oinaion)': 'the Greeks spoke Greek and the Romeyka dialect'; no scholarly dialect source seen
others: Muslim majority; Armenian (c. 700 in town, 7,700 in the kaza, 1914, Kévorkian 2011); American Protestant mission from 1866
population: 3905 persons (1896) [Trabzon salname 1896, whole kaza (7.4% of 52,507) (as cited on Wikipedia) tr 'Ünye'] | 4000 persons (1902) [PW 'Unye (Oinaion)', plate caption, no source] | 3074 persons [Trabzon salnames, town of 9,161 ('early 20th century') (as cited on Wikipedia) tr 'Ünye'] | 7600 persons (1911) [1911 Greek survey 'Greek villages in Pontos', via VGM: whole kaza, 19 communities, 15 schools, 4 churches] | 6200 persons (1911) [Alexandris 1999; Lazaridis, Αρχείον Πόντου 16 (1988), via PW 'Unye (Oinaion)': Ünye county 1910-12] | 2500 persons (1914) [VGM Kaza Ünye; PW 'Unye (Oinaion)' (town, of c. 10,000)] | 800 families (1870) [Ioannidis 1870, p. 205, Part Β′ «Στατιστικὴ τῆς χώρας» (chs. Η′–Ι′)]
churches: St Nicholas and Holy Trinity (parish churches 1914); Dormition (standing 1930); medieval chapel of St Nicholas at Ayanikola, 3 km west
fate_1914_1923: Deportation of the community began in July 1917 and went on at intervals: gendarmes beat and robbed the people and scattered them between Kastamonu, Zile and elsewhere; many hid in the woods for months and 300 reached Trebizond and Russia (Patriarchate 1919, p. 126; printed 'Ounia'). 1916: c. 500 (VGM: 520) Greek hostages taken in the Ünye area and killed after guerrillas escaped from Keris; villages burned (VGM; PW). Oct 1916: a brigade sent against the Ünye area burned eleven Greek villages (Saltsis, via VGM Kaza Niksar). Jan 1917: c. 60 notables marched to Amasya, half died in ten days (Ioannidou 2016). 1917: Greeks deported inland to Tokat, Sivas and Amasya, most died of hunger and cold (VGM); July 1917 deportation, c. 300 escaped to Russian-held Trebizond (Patriarchate 1919). 16 Jun 1921: 101 men marched to Tokat (Hionides 1996). Sep 1921: most Christian men massacred, women and boys deported (Black Book 1922). Osman Ağa's bands in the kaza (Black Book, via greek-genocide.net). April 1923: the last Greeks left, one ship carrying 362 (Ioannidou 2016).
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

fate_1914_1923: On 27 December [1916] 80 leading Greeks were arrested and sent inland, the people of the upper town and Eliaz-keuy (about 4,000) were seized and marched over snowy mountains, 40 more notables were taken on 1 January and about 300 notables and merchants expelled in all, with arrests on 10-11 January and expulsions on the 13th (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 120–121; printed 'Amassia'; probable identification: the passage is the Greek Legation's Samsun report (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 48-50) almost word for word: 'Amassia' renders Amisos (Samsun), 'upper Amassia (Kadi Mahalessi)' is Upper Samsun (Cadikioi), 'Karak' is Kavak and 'Kavza... eighty kilometres distant' is Havza; read literally it would be Amasya). Dec 1916: the town was encircled, residents ordered to the centre and held in barracks, then marched inland; deportees seen at Kavak, Havza and Çorum (Greek legation report, 27 Dec 1916, via greek-genocide.net); deportations resumed 17-18 Jan 1917 (with Bafra); Refet Pasha reported 13,406 Rums sent inland from Samsun (BOA DH.ŞFR 548/1, 12 Mar 1917, via Biber). 1921: Topal Osman's bands entered Samsun in late May; on 16 June 1921 Ankara ordered the deportation of all Greek males 16-50 (about 21,000 deported 1921-22 per Shenk); first convoy left 16-17 June and was attacked at Kavak; 1,500 women and children from nearby villages deported in Sept 1921, 700 in Nov 1921, 1,300 in Apr 1922 (US Navy reports, via Shenk / Wikipedia). Survivors left by sea under the exchange, 1923-24.

churches: Greek church with a courtyard (Black Book 1922); names not found
fate_1914_1923: Threatening posters, levies and forced billeting of immigrants in 1914; its Christians expelled at intervals [1917]; arms given to Turkish peasants in October 1917 (Ilias, son-in-law of Kutchuk Yorghi, killed); an order of 16 December 1917 gave ten days before deportation to 'Amassia' in midwinter (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 119, 121, 124; printed 'Bafra'). 1916-17: the deportations of 17-18 Jan 1917 included Greeks from Bafra (greek-genocide.net, after the American Hellenic Society 1918); Bafra Rums were sent to Bolu in 1917 (Biber); Bafra was evacuated on 5 Feb 1917 (Fotiadis 2019, via Topalidis). 1921: on 5/18 June troops and paramilitaries surrounded the town and took the men (Black Book; Morris & Ze'evi 2019: 408); the local Greek elite were lured to a dinner and killed and seven priests were killed with axes (Morris & Ze'evi: 408); convoys of 500-600 left Bafra on 17, 21 and 24 June (Biber, after Yerasimos); the Black Book's eyewitness says the convoys were killed in the churches of Elezli (Suludere, c. 535), Selemelik (c. 500) and 'Kodje-sou' (680); about 6,000 women and children were expelled on 31 Aug and 2,500 on 19 Sept 1921, and a column of 4,000 Bafra women and children was met near Sivas (Morris & Ze'evi: 408); 17 orphans died of hunger in the Bafra orphanage (Black Book). Totals: 14,010 deported from Bafra, at least 9,140 killed (Gavriilidis 1924, via Topalidis). Named by the Black Book as responsible: the kaymakam 'Zemil Bey', the notables 'Nevrisin Mehmet' and 'Tiralizate Mehmet', and Osman Ağa. 1922-24: Christians shipped out of the Samsun area (10,460 in Nov 1922, Fotiadis via Topalidis) and in the exchange.
turkish_account: notes_turkish_account: Biber (Turkish archival study) reports Rum bands burning 'Koçhisar' in Bafra and the 'Sakızcı' quarter (statement of Yusuf Kemal), Rums gathering on Nebyan Dağı (government disarmament postponed 12 Jan 1921) and Central Army clashes there.
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

language_basis: No village-level source on the language was found. Triandafyllidis (1938) puts the western (Oinountiac) Pontic group in a 'non-contiguous' zone from İnebolu to Ünye, and Tompaidis (1992) says that zone was broken by Turkish-speaking populations, so both Pontic- and Turkish-speaking Orthodox are possible here.
population: 526 persons (1922) [Black Book 1922, Amassia statistics, 'Tikendjik' (pre-persecution population as claimed)] |  (1992) [listed without figure in the CAMS list (Samouilidis 1992), pontosworld 165-bafra]
fate_1914_1923: The army set it on fire and forced its people out (March [1917]) (Patriarchate 1919, p. 123; printed 'Dikedjik'; probable identification: Dikencik, Black Book 'Tikendjik'). No record for this village by name. For the Bafra kaza as a whole: Dec 1916-Feb 1917 villagers of the Bafra hinterland were deported or sent 'to wander from one village to another' (Morris & Ze'evi 2019: 390-391); Metropolitan Germanos reported 8 Greek villages near Bafra burned in the week of 5 Feb 1917, names not given (Fotiadis 2019: 240, via Topalidis 2022); Greek guerrillas (andartes) were active in the Bafra hills and on Nebyan Dağı from 1916, as a largely defensive force (Psomiades 2006, via Topalidis); the Central Army (formed 9 Dec 1920 under Nurettin Paşa) collected weapons and destroyed villages (Biber, from Turkish archives); June-Sept 1921 men aged 15-50 were deported (decree of 16 June 1921, Biber) and then women and children, with massacres (Morris & Ze'evi 2019: 407-409); Feb 1922 Turkish forces under Fethi combed the Bafra hinterland for Greeks hiding in the mountains (Morris & Ze'evi: 409). Survivors left in the exchange (1923-24).
turkish_account: fate_turkish_account: On the Turkish side, a statement by Yusuf Kemal says Rum bands burned Koçhisar in Bafra and the Sakızcı quarter; the Central Army fought the bands, and the villages it destroyed are described as villages that supported them (Biber, from Turkish archives).
evidence: Named in more than one source.

language_basis: 1911 consular census as printed in K&A 1984 Table VI, row 324 (by ditto mark, as printed)
population: 1516 persons (1922) [Black Book 1922, Amassia statistics, 'Aladjam (mudirlik)' (pre-persecution population as claimed)] | 1516 persons (1911) [K&A 1984, Table VI row 324 ('Alaçam')]
fate_1914_1923: Evacuated with its neighbouring villages under the order of the end of July 1916 (Patriarchate 1919, p. 119; printed 'Aladjam'). Evacuated by February 1917: 'Aladjan' is in the Greek Legation's list of the Samsun-district villages emptied of their Greeks, all those of the coast as far as Alaçam (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 68–69; probable identification: Alaçam (Black Book Aladjam)). Deportation convoys left Alaçam on 18, 21 and 22 June 1921, the third of about 1,000 people (Biber, after Yerasimos). The Black Book (report of 25 Sept 1921) says the last 1,600 women and children were deported inland via 'Boivat' (Boyabat) towards Osmancık and that most died on the way. The Patriarchate reported seven priests of Alaçam, Bafra and nearby villages crucified in the Gözköy market (Morris & Ze'evi 2019: 417). Survivors left in the exchange (1923-24).
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

fate_1914_1923: Evacuated under an order of the end of July 1916; after eight days' march the people reached Kastamonu and were sent on to Taşköprü, Boyabat and Safranbolu, and a fire destroyed 400 Greek houses and shops (Patriarchate 1919, p. 119; printed 'Sinope'). 1916: the German consul Kuckhoff reported 'the entire Greek population of Sinope and the coastal region of the district of Kastamonu has been exiled' (Travis 2017, cited in Wikipedia, 'Pontic Greek genocide'). Sept-Oct 1921: Christian children aged 9-12 rounded up and deported from Sinop and Gerze (Morris & Ze'evi 2019: 411). The Black Book (1922) counts about 4,000 women and boys alive 'in Sinope and the Interland'. 1923-24: exchange; many settled in Nea Sinopi.
evidence: Well documented: several independent sources, with figures.

fate_1914_1923: 18 Jan 1921: arrests of the Greek men of the district, incl. Bishop Efthymios of Zela (assistant to the metropolitan) and the chancellor Platon Aivazidis (VGM citing Fotiadis). Efthymios died in Amasya prison (29 May 1921). The Amasya Independence Tribunal sat 20 Aug-21 Sep 1921; 72 Greeks incl. Platon were hanged in the town square on 8/21 Sep 1921 (Fotiadis via VGM);wikipedia 'Amasya trials'). The named victims include men of Samsun, Bafra and Merzifon, so the trials concern the whole metropolis, not only Amasya. Remaining Orthodox left in the exchange (VGM: 'all Greeks were forcibly removed during the 1923 population exchange').

Samsun 1902), three other officers of the college's 'Pontus' club and Prof. Theocharides arrested, tried at Amasya and hanged; Wikipedia names the former faculty Ch. Evstathiades, G. Lamprianos and D. Theocharides among those hanged at Amasya. From 13 Jul 1921: Topal Osman's men killed the men; women and children were sent to a Greek mining town c. 20 km away (VGM: 'Metallion-Sim', probably Gümüş Maden); c. 1,000 Greeks and Armenians killed in four days (VGM), c. 1,200 of 2,000 Christians (The Times), 5,000 Greeks of Merzifon and Havza (Central Council of Pontus, advocacy). 27, 30 and 31 Aug 1921: deportations of 1,230, 1,650 and 1,284 Christians, mostly women and children, towards Elazığ, Bitlis and Van.
